1	\subsection{NG-16: replacing a tilted mean by a deterministic value}
2	\label{S:nogo-16}
3	
4	The Gaussian density cost is exact. A loss may instead enter when the
5	random solution under the tilted law is replaced by a deterministic
6	surrogate. The following two calculations identify the loss without
7	asserting an obstruction to Gaussian shifts themselves.
8	
9	\setcounter{nogo}{15}
10	\begin{nogo}[A deterministic surrogate can lose the annealed factor]
11	  \label{P:nogo-16}
12	  Let $A>0$, $c>0$ and $0<r<2$, and define
13	  \[
14	    J_c=\sup_{H\ge0}\{cAH^r-H^2/2\}.
15	  \]
16	  Then $J_c=c^{2/(2-r)}J_1$, whereas
17	  \[
18	    \sup_{H\ge0}\{2AH^r-H^2\}=2J_1<J_2.
19	  \]
20	  Moreover, for $Y=e^{\sigma Z}$, $Z$ standard Gaussian and $\sigma>0$,
21	  the full tilted-mean Cauchy--Schwarz bound recovers $\E Y^2$ exactly,
22	  while substituting $Y(h)=e^{\sigma h}$ loses a factor in its logarithm.
23	\end{nogo}
24	\begin{proof}
25	  Substitute $H=c^{1/(2-r)}K$ in the definition of $J_c$. Both terms
26	  acquire the factor $c^{2/(2-r)}$. The supremum $J_1$ is finite, since
27	  $r<2$, and positive, since for small positive $H$ the positive term
28	  dominates. Factoring two from the surrogate score proves the strict
29	  comparison because $2/(2-r)>1$.
30	
31	  Let $Q_h$ be the Gaussian shift with density
32	  $L_h=e^{hZ-h^2/2}$ relative to the standard Gaussian law. Then
33	  $\E L_h^2=e^{h^2}$, so Cauchy--Schwarz gives
34	  \[
35	    \E Y^2\ge(\E_{Q_h}Y)^2e^{-h^2}.
36	  \]
37	  The exact tilted mean is $\E_{Q_h}Y=e^{\sigma^2/2+\sigma h}$.
38	  Maximizing its resulting exponent
39	  $\sigma^2+2\sigma h-h^2$ at $h=\sigma$ gives
40	  $e^{2\sigma^2}=\E Y^2$. Substitution of the deterministic value
41	  $Y(h)$ instead gives the maximum $e^{\sigma^2}$.
42	  This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-16}.
43	\end{proof}
44	
45	These are generic scalar score calculations, not an SPDE no-go. They
46	identify which term is lost and show that retaining the full tilted mean
47	can avoid the loss. A deterministic surrogate remains useful if one
48	proves that its error is negligible on the intended exponential scale;
49	without such an estimate it cannot identify the annealed constant.
50

1	\subsection{NG-13: angular smoothing and isotropic envelopes}\label{S:nogo-13}
2	
3	Smooth angular densities admit finite angular suprema. It is tempting to
4	approximate a singular covariance by such densities and apply the Riesz
5	estimate with that supremum as amplitude. The limit below shows why the
6	amplitudes cannot remain bounded.
7	
8	\setcounter{nogo}{12}
9	\begin{nogo}[No uniform isotropic envelope for a plane covariance]
10	  \label{P:nogo-13}
11	  In $\mathbb R^3=\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R$ set
12	  \[
13	    \Gamma(\ud y,\ud z)=\frac1{2\pi}|y|^{-1/2}\ud y\,\delta_0(\ud z).
14	  \]
15	  This is an admissible covariance with $\alpha=3/2$ and
16	  $\alpha_0=1/4$. If nonnegative measures $\Gamma_n$ converge vaguely to
17	  $\Gamma$ and satisfy
18	  \[
19	    \Gamma_n(\ud x)\le C_n|x|^{-3/2}\ud x,
20	  \]
21	  then $C_n\to\infty$.
22	\end{nogo}
23	\begin{proof}
24	  The planar Riesz factor is locally integrable and positive definite by
25	  its Gaussian mixture representation. The normal Dirac covariance is
26	  positive definite: in its quadratic form the two normal coordinates
27	  coincide, leaving an integral of nonnegative tangential quadratic
28	  forms. Thus, the product is positive definite. For every $r>0$ and
29	  Borel set $A$, the substitution $y=ry'$ in its defining integral gives
30	  $\Gamma(rA)=r^{2-1/2}\Gamma(A)=r^{3/2}\Gamma(A)$. Its finite mass on
31	  a radius $R$ ball is proportional to $R^{3/2}$; polynomial mass growth
32	  also gives temperedness.
33	
34	  Suppose a subsequence of $C_n$ were bounded by $C<\infty$. For every
35	  nonnegative compactly supported continuous $f$, vague convergence gives
36	  \[
37	    \int f\ud\Gamma=\lim_n\int f\ud\Gamma_n
38	    \le C\int f(x)|x|^{-3/2}\ud x.
39	  \]
40	  This is measure domination, so $\Gamma$ would be absolutely continuous
41	  with respect to three-dimensional Lebesgue measure. But the compact
42	  planar annulus $\{(y,0):1\le|y|\le2\}$ has positive $\Gamma$ mass and
43	  zero Lebesgue measure. This contradiction excludes every bounded
44	  subsequence, proving the asserted limit.
45	  This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-13}.
46	\end{proof}
47	
48	This argument applies in particular to angular smoothing whenever the
49	smoothed covariances converge to the plane measure. It requires no
50	ellipsoid representation. It rules out a uniform scalar isotropic density
51	envelope, not other covariance majorants or density of any proposed cone.
52	The reopening condition is an estimate that remains uniform without taking
53	an angular supremum, or a comparison adapted to the singular support.
54

1	\subsection[NG-18: an oversized middle-cross envelope]{NG-18: erasing the middle-cross shift makes an envelope too large}
2	\label{S:nogo-18}
3	
4	A later white-space comparison retains four vertices and a middle cross
5	pair. Removing the clock-overlap penalty gives a positive upper bound.
6	One further simplification, erasing the shift of its root kernel, also
7	increases the bound, but increases it beyond the comparator at an explicit
8	parameter point. This is an obstruction to closing that envelope, not a
9	counterexample to the original comparison.
10	
11	\setcounter{nogo}{17}
12	\begin{nogo}[The shift-erased envelope is not below the wave transform]
13	  \label{P:nogo-18}
14	  Consider the white $(1,3)$ diagram with middle-cross partition $02\cdot13$,
15	  common gap damping one, cross rate $\lambda\ge0$ and self rate $\nu\ge0$.
16	  Put $b=1+\nu$, $c=1+\lambda$, $A=\lambda+\lambda^2/2$. Its actual wave
17	  transform $I$ and the shift-erased clock upper envelope $M_b(0;A)$ satisfy
18	  at $b=1,c=11/10$
19	  \[
20	    I=\frac{545}{11616},\qquad M_b(0;A)=\frac{1025}{21483},\qquad
21	    I-M_b(0;A)=-\frac{6005}{7562016}<0.
22	  \]
23	  Consequently the proposed pointwise closure $M_b(0;A)\le I$ is false.
24	\end{nogo}
25	\begin{proof}
26	  We give the integral identifications so that the rational test specifies
27	  which bound fails. With singleton gap $u$ and long-chain gaps $v,w,z$,
28	  the spatial factor is
29	  $\int G_u(X)G_v(Y)G_w(X-Y)G_z(Y-X)\,\ud X\ud Y$.
30	  Set $R=u+v$, $q=u-v$. Integration in $R$, including its Jacobian,
31	  gives the exact wave expression
32	  \[
33	    I=\frac1{16}\int_{w,z>0}\int_{\mathbb R}
34	    e^{-b(w+z)-\lambda|q-w|}
35	    \int_0^{\min(w,z)}e^{-\max(|q|,t)}\,\ud t\ud q\ud w\ud z.
36	  \]
37	  To check the spatial reduction, the derivative of the area
38	  $\{|X|<u,|Y|<v,|X-Y|<C\}$ with respect to $C$ is
39	  $2(R-\max(C,|q|))_+$; the area vanishes at $C=0$.
40	  Integrate this against $e^{-R}/32$ for $R>|q|$.
41	  Next integrate $z\ge t$ and put $w=t+x$. Splitting the remaining $q$
42	  integral into $q<0$, $0\le q\le t$, and $q\ge t$ gives respectively
43	  \[
44	    \frac{1/c+1/(2b+\lambda+1)}{16b(b+\lambda)(2b+2\lambda+1)},\quad
45	    \frac1{16b(b+\lambda)(2b+1)(2b+1+\lambda)},
46	  \]
47	  \[
48	    \frac{1/(b+\lambda)+1/c}{16b(2b+1)(b+1)}.
49	  \]
50	  Adding gives
51	  \[
52	    I=\frac{2b^2+4bc+2c^2-c+1}
53	    {8bc(b+1)(2b+1)(b+c-1)(2b+2c-1)}.
54	  \]
55	
56	  For the clock envelope write $h(r)=(2\pi r)^{-1/2}$ and
57	  $m(s)=1/(\pi\sqrt2\sqrt{s-1/2})$, $s>1/2$.
58	  The two spatial pair differences have covariance matrix
59	  $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}u+v+w&-w\\-w&w+z\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
60	  Writing $r=w+z$, its determinant is $rR+wz$, so their joint white
61	  density factors as $h(r)h(R+wz/r)$. After deleting the nonnegative
62	  clock-overlap penalty, the root kernel is
63	  \[
64	    H_\gamma(q)=\int_{|q|}^\infty e^{-R/2}h(R+\gamma)\,\ud R
65	    =\int_{1/2}^\infty\frac{m(s)}s
66	    e^{-(s-1/2)\gamma}e^{-s|q|}\,\ud s,
67	    \qquad \gamma=\frac{wz}{r}.
68	  \]
69	  The equality follows from the positive Gamma integral for $h$.
70	  The convolution of the mixture component $q\mapsto e^{-s|q|}$ with
71	  $q\mapsto e^{-A|q|}$, evaluated at $w$, equals $2S_{A,s}(w)/(s+A)$, where
72	  \[
73	    S_{A,s}(w)=e^{-Aw}+\int_0^w A e^{-At}e^{-s(w-t)}\,\ud t\le1.
74	  \]
75	  The inequality follows by bounding $e^{-s(w-t)}$ by one; the remaining
76	  integral is $1-e^{-Aw}$.
77	  Replacing $S$ by one is precisely the shift erasure. More generally, for
78	  $\eta\ge0$, replacing it by $e^{-\eta w}$ defines
79	  \[
80	    M_b(\eta;A)=\frac1{16}\int_{1/2}^\infty
81	    \frac{m(s)}{s(s+A)}\int_0^\infty h(r)e^{-b^2r/2}
82	    \int_0^r e^{-(s-1/2)w(r-w)/r-\eta w}\,\ud w\ud r\ud s.
83	  \]
84	  All integrals here are positive. Set $w=rt$ and $\tau=s-1/2$.
85	  For $\eta,\tau\ge0$, put $p=\sqrt{b^2+2\eta}$. The elementary bridge
86	  integral is
87	  \[
88	    \int_0^1[b^2+2\eta t+2\tau t(1-t)]^{-3/2}\,\ud t
89	    =\frac{2(p+b)}{bp((p+b)^2+2\tau)}.
90	  \]
91	  It follows by integrating a quadratic power; at $\eta=\tau=0$ both sides
92	  are $b^{-3}$. Substitution $z=\sqrt{2s-1}$ and partial fractions give
93	  \begin{align*}
94	    M_b(\eta;A)&=\frac{p+b}{2\pi bp}
95	    \int_0^\infty\frac{\ud z}
96	    {(z^2+1)(z^2+c^2)(z^2+(p+b)^2)}\\
97	    &=\frac{1+c+p+b}{4bp c(c+1)(c+p+b)(1+p+b)}.
98	  \end{align*}
99	  The usual identity $\int_0^\infty(z^2+q^2)^{-1}\ud z=\pi/(2q)$
100	  proves the partial fraction evaluation; coincident rates follow by
101	  continuity. At $\eta=0$, $p=b$. Substituting the asserted rational
102	  parameters in these two expressions gives the displayed strict gap.
103	  This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-18}.
104	\end{proof}
105	
106	The boundary value $\nu=0$ is a legitimate fixed-parameter transform;
107	continuity of both rational expressions also gives an overshoot for some
108	$\nu>0$ nearby. The no-go does not refute $J\le I$, where $J$ is the
109	original shared-clock candidate, nor does it decide an integrated
110	comparison using this envelope. The surviving middle-cross comparison
111	retains $S_{A,1/2}(w)$, instead of replacing it by one, and obtains a smaller
112	envelope. Reopening this particular closure requires keeping a shift cost
113	or proving a different integrated estimate. The historical standalone
114	record was not separately adjudicated; the subsequent accepted
115	middle-cross analysis and this reconstructed proof do not change that
116	historical review status.

1	\subsection{NG-19: discarding an independent Gaussian residual}
2	\label{S:nogo-19}
3	
4	An orthogonal Gaussian projection produces an independent residual with
5	positive semidefinite covariance. This makes projection a useful change-of-law
6	tool. It does not give pointwise nonnegative residual covariance, and the
7	wave mean need not increase when that residual is restored.
8	
9	\setcounter{nogo}{18}
10	\begin{nogo}[A positive semidefinite residual can lower the wave mean]
11	  \label{P:nogo-19}
12	  There is an admissible one-dimensional parent covariance $C$ and an
13	  actual rank-one Gaussian projection with covariance $P$ such that
14	  $C-P$ is positive semidefinite but
15	  \[
16	    \E u_C(h;1,0)<\E u_P(h;1,0)
17	  \]
18	  for all sufficiently small positive noise couplings $h$. The projection
19	  $P$ is not asserted to be stationary or homogeneous.
20	\end{nogo}
21	\begin{proof}
22	  Put $a=99/100$ and
23	  \[
24	    C((s,x),(t,y))=(1-a)|s-t|^{-a}|x-y|^{-1/2}.
25	  \]
26	  Its spatial degree is $\alpha=1/2$, and $\alpha+a<2$. Gaussian mixtures
27	  of the two power kernels verify positive definiteness and local
28	  integrability. Let $\psi(s,x)=\mathbf1_{[0,1]}(s)\mathbf1_{[-1,1]}(x)$,
29	  and $V=\E W(\psi)^2$. The indicator is a legal Hilbert-space test by
30	  bounded smooth approximation and dominated convergence. Local integrability
31	  and positivity of $C$ give $0<V<\infty$. Put $Z=W(\psi)/\sqrt V$ and
32	  define the covariance profile by the locally integrable kernel formula
33	  \[
34	    m(s,x)=\frac1{\sqrt V}\int_0^1\int_{-1}^1
35	    C((s,x),(r,y))\ud y\ud r.
36	  \]
37	  For every smooth compactly supported spacetime test $f$, Fubini's
38	  theorem identifies $\langle m,f\rangle=\E[W(f)Z]$.
39	  Thus, $m$ is the covariance of the generalized field with $Z$; no
40	  pointwise random variable $W(s,x)$ is used. Gaussian projection gives
41	  $W=Zm+W^\perp$ with $W^\perp$ independent of $Z$ and
42	  covariance $C-P$, where $P=m\otimes m$. Cauchy--Schwarz gives its
43	  positive semidefiniteness.
44	
45	  Direct integration gives, on $0\le s\le1$,
46	  \[
47	    E_\phi=\frac{16\sqrt2}{3},\quad V=\frac{2E_\phi}{2-a},\quad
48	    m(s,x)=\frac{B_a(s)F(x)}{\sqrt V},
49	  \]
50	  where $B_a(s)=s^{1-a}+(1-s)^{1-a}\ge1$ and
51	  $F(x)=\int_{-1}^1|x-y|^{-1/2}\ud y$. We have $F\le4$ everywhere and
52	  $F(x)\ge2\sqrt2$ for $|x|\le1$. Thus, $m$ is bounded and nonnegative,
53	  and $m(s,x)m(t,y)\ge8/V$ on the backward cone of $(1,0)$.
54	
55	  For a covariance $D$ the degree-two ordinary mean coefficient is
56	  \[
57	    A_D=\int_{0<s<t<1}\int_{\mathbb R^2}
58	    G_{1-t}(-y)G_{t-s}(y-z)D((s,z),(t,y))
59	    \ud z\ud y\ud s\ud t.
60	  \]
61	  This is the single self-pair term of Proposition~\ref{P:mixed}; there
62	  is no additional factorial. With $G_r(x)=\mathbf1_{\{|x|<r\}}/2$,
63	  integration of the parent covariance yields
64	  \[
65	    A_C=\frac{1-a}{1-\alpha}
66	    \frac1{(2-\alpha-a)(3-\alpha-a)(4-\alpha-a)}
67	    =\frac{20000}{1932951}<\frac1{96}.
68	  \]
69	  For covariance one the same integral is
70	  $\int_{0<s<t<1}(1-t)(t-s)\ud s\ud t=1/24$. Therefore,
71	  \[
72	    A_P\ge\frac{8}{24V}
73	    =\frac{101}{3200\sqrt2}>\frac1{48}.
74	  \]
75	
76	  We justify passage from coefficients to full means. Write the parent
77	  solution as $u_C(h)=\sum_{n\ge0}h^nX_n$. For any fixed $r>1$,
78	  finiteness of the second moment at amplified covariance $r^2C$ and
79	  nonnegativity of the mixed moments in Proposition~\ref{P:mixed} give
80	  \[
81	    \|X_n\|_2\le \sqrt{B_r}\,r^{-n},\qquad
82	    B_r=\E|u_C(r;1,0)|^2<\infty.
83	  \]
84	  Hence, the $L^2$ norm of the tail starting at $n=4$ is at most
85	  $\sqrt{B_r}(|h|/r)^4/(1-|h|/r)$. Odd means vanish by Gaussian sign
86	  symmetry, giving $\E u_C(h)=1+h^2A_C+O(h^4)$.
87	
88	  For $P$, the potential is the bounded profile $Zm$. If $M=\sup|m|$,
89	  the deterministic Picard coefficients at time one are bounded by
90	  $M^n/(2n)!$. The absolute mean series for $|h|\le1$ is bounded by
91	  $\E\cosh\sqrt{M|Z|}<\infty$. Factoring $h^4$ from its tail and
92	  using symmetry therefore gives $\E u_P(h)=1+h^2A_P+O(h^4)$.
93	  The strict coefficient gap proves the claimed inequality.
94	  This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-19}.
95	\end{proof}
96	
97	The same distinction persists under a variance tilt of the projected
98	coordinate. For $1<q<2$, its density relative to the parent law is
99	\[
100	  L_q(Z)=q^{-1/2}\exp\bigl((1-q^{-1})Z^2/2\bigr),\qquad
101	  \E L_q^2=[q(2-q)]^{-1/2}.
102	\]
103	The equivalent Gaussian law has covariance $Q=C+(q-1)P$. The same original
104	measurable solution has an $O(h^4)$ mean remainder under this law by
105	Cauchy--Schwarz and the preceding $L^2$ tail estimate. Its degree-two
106	coefficient is $A_Q=A_C+(q-1)A_P<qA_P-1/96$. This is an equivalent-law
107	statement, not a new stationary-model existence theorem for $Q$.
108	To identify its degree-two coefficient, one can use the same regularization
109	as the parent construction. If $K_\delta$ denotes the truncated temporal
110	covariance and $p_\epsilon$ the spatial heat kernel, its cross-covariance
111	with $Z$ is
112	\[
113	  m_{\epsilon,\delta}(s,x)
114	  =\frac{(1-a)\int_0^1K_\delta(s-r)\ud r}{\sqrt V}
115	  (p_\epsilon*F)(x).
116	\]
117	The bounds $0\le K_\delta\le|\,\cdot\,|^{-a}$ and $F\le4$ give
118	$0\le m_{\epsilon,\delta}\le8/\sqrt V$. These profiles converge to
119	$m$ at interior times. Dominated convergence on the finite-mass terminal
120	wave kernel identifies the added $P$ contribution. The parent degree-two
121	term converges in $L^2$, and $L_q\in L^2$ transfers its expectation to the
122	equivalent law. Thus, the fixed-order Gaussian covariance identity indeed
123	gives the stated $A_Q$, without invoking a homogeneous representation for
124	$Q$. Consequently, discarding the residual also fails in this tilted comparison.
125	A large-time bridge for specially chosen projections could still hold,
126	but it must be proved at the required scale. Positive semidefinite order
127	alone cannot supply it.

1	\subsection{NG-33: check the mathematics returned by a reviewer}
2	\label{S:nogo-33}
3	
4	A review report is also a mathematical argument and can contain an incorrect
5	step. This historical record groups three such checks. The manuscript had
6	the correct expressions; the examples below explain why the proposed review
7	steps could not replace them. These are not three new counterexamples to the
8	stochastic model.
9	
10	\setcounter{nogo}{32}
11	\begin{nogo}[Three invalid proof steps]\label{P:nogo-33}
12	  The following assertions fail.
13	  \begin{enumerate}
14	    \item The free phase matrix
15	      $S_0(t)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$
16	      is a contraction in the Euclidean norm for every $t\ge0$.
17	    \item For $x>0$, an integer $n\ge1$ and $0<\vartheta<1$, the series term
18	      $x^n/(n!)^\vartheta$ equals
19	      $A_nB_n$, where
20	      \[
21	        A_n=\frac{(2x^{1/\vartheta})^n}{n!},\qquad
22	        B_n=2^{-\vartheta n/(1-\vartheta)}.
23	      \]
24	    \item The denominator $k!\,k^{(2-\alpha)k}$ may always be replaced by
25	      the larger denominator $(k!)^3$ in the coefficient bound of
26	      Proposition~\ref{P:low-alpha-upper}.
27	  \end{enumerate}
28	\end{nogo}
29	
30	\begin{proof}
31	  The vector $(0,1)$ has norm one, but its image under $S_0(t)$ has norm
32	  $\sqrt{1+t^2}>1$ for $t>0$. To transfer this to the whole-space phase,
33	  use exactly the inhomogeneous Sobolev norm of
34	  Section~\ref{S:wave-variance}: $E=H^{1/2}\times H^{-1/2}$ and
35	  $J_0=\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda^{1/2},\Lambda^{-1/2})$, where
36	  $\Lambda=(1-\Delta)^{1/2}$. With $r=|\xi|$ and
37	  $\langle\xi\rangle=\sqrt{1+r^2}$, the Fourier symbol of
38	  $J_0S(t)J_0^{-1}$ is
39	  \[
40	    \begin{pmatrix}
41	      \cos(tr)&\langle\xi\rangle\sin(tr)/r\\
42	      -r\sin(tr)/\langle\xi\rangle&\cos(tr)
43	    \end{pmatrix}
44	    \longrightarrow S_0(t)\qquad(r\downarrow0).
45	  \]
46	  Choose normalized Fourier bumps supported in balls shrinking to zero
47	  and place them in the second coordinate of $J_0z$. Continuity of this
48	  matrix at zero shows that their image norms tend to $\sqrt{1+t^2}$.
49	  Thus $S(t)$ is not a contraction on this $E$. The distinction between
50	  $\langle\xi\rangle$ and $|\xi|$ matters: this is not a claim about the
51	  homogeneous energy norm. The valid estimate keeps a free-growth factor.
52	
53	  The correct identity in the second assertion is
54	  $x^n/(n!)^\vartheta=A_n^\vartheta B_n^{1-\vartheta}$.
55	  At $\vartheta=3/4$, $n=1$ and $x=1$, its left side is one, whereas
56	  $A_1B_1=2\cdot(1/8)=1/4$. H\"older applies to the weighted product, as
57	  in the proof of Proposition~\ref{P:static-phase-all-orders}.
58	
59	  For the third assertion choose the permitted spatial-white value
60	  $\alpha=1$ and $k=3$. Then $k!k^{(2-\alpha)k}=162<216=(k!)^3$.
61	  For $M>0$, an upper bound $M/162$ does not imply the smaller upper bound
62	  $M/216$.
63	  The valid factorial weakening is instead
64	  \[
65	    k!k^{(2-\alpha)k}\ge(k!)^{3-\alpha},
66	  \]
67	  since $k!\le k^k$ and $2-\alpha>0$; at this example its right side is
68	  $36$. This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-33}.
69	\end{proof}
70	
71	\paragraph{Scope and what survives.}
72	The last arithmetic check refutes an inference between numerical bounds;
73	it does not prove that the actual coefficient exceeds $M/216$.
74	All three corrected arguments remain in the main text. Their lesson is to
75	check an asserted derivation against its domains, factors and quantifiers,
76	even when the report containing it has a favorable overall verdict.
77	
78	\paragraph{What would permit the discarded steps?}
79	Contractivity needs a suitable invariant norm or a restricted state class.
80	The H\"older factors need their conjugate powers. A stronger factorial
81	bound needs an additional estimate; it cannot be obtained by changing the
82	exponent in the denominator.

1	\begin{hypothesis}[Homogeneous covariance]\label{H:homog}
2	  Let $d \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $0 < \alpha_0 < 1$. The spatial covariance is a
3	  nonnegative, even, positive-definite tempered Radon measure $\Gamma$ on
4	  $\R^d$, with positive even tempered Radon spectral measure $\mu$ in the
5	  convention
6	  \[
7	    \Gamma=\int e^{i\xi\cdot x}\mu(\ud\xi)
8	    \quad\text{in the sense of tempered distributions}.
9	  \]
10	  The symbol $\gamma$ in~\eqref{E:cov} denotes this covariance as a function
11	  when one exists, and as a distribution otherwise. For every Borel set $A$ and
12	  $c > 0$, $\Gamma(cA) = c^{d-\alpha}\Gamma(A)$, and
13	  \begin{equation}\label{E:threshold}
14	    \alpha_0+\alpha<2,
15	  \end{equation}
16	  with $0 < \alpha < d$, or $\alpha = d = 1$. In particular, the last case
17	  includes spatial white noise $\Gamma = \delta_0$.

135	  Schwartz $f,g$, let $Z_n^\epsilon(h)$ be the $n$th regularized static Duhamel

138	  self-contractions; it is not a pure Wick chaos. There is an explicit finite
139	  constant

142	  \]
143	  such that, for $n \ge 1$, uniformly in $\epsilon > 0$,
144	  \begin{equation}\label{E:all-static-phase-orders}
145	    \|Z_n^\epsilon(h)\|_{L^2(\Omega;X_{1/h})}
146	    \le
147	    \frac{(A_\alpha\sqrt{R_\alpha})^n
148	    h^{(4-\alpha)n/2}}{(n!)^{(3-\alpha)/2}}
149	    \|(f,g)\|_{1/h}.

152	  $\sum_{n\ge0}\sigma^nZ_n^\epsilon(h)$ converges in $L^2$ phase. Its squared

164	  positive-order term is zero. Assume $R_\alpha > 0$. First work at finite
165	  Gaussian cutoff $m$, degree cutoff $N$ and spatial band $b$, with initial
166	  phase $S_b(f,g)$ times the Gaussian vacuum $1$. All relevant operators are

172	  $\cos(h\sqrt L)$ and $\sin(h\sqrt L)/\sqrt L$ of a bounded $L$. Cauchy's

174	  \[

176	    \left(\frac{d_N}
177	    {\delta_{\alpha/2}\lambda^{2-\alpha/2}}\right)^n
178	    \|S_b(f,g)\|_\lambda .
179	  \]

181	  Lemma~\ref{L:finite-word-cutoff} with one color, $N = n$, the spatial phase
182	  Hilbert space as $\mathscr{X}$, and its free wave operators as the $F_l$. It
183	  identifies each cutoff Duhamel word exactly with its uncompressed word,
184	  including self-contractions. Dominated time integration preserves this
185	  identity.

188	  $\|(f,g)\|_{n/h} \le \|(f,g)\|_{1/h}$. Also $d_n \le

190	  \[

193	    n^{-(3-\alpha)n/2}\|(f,g)\|_{1/h}.

302	  $\boldsymbol\epsilon$,
303	  \begin{equation}\label{E:d1-spatial-product}
304	    S_{D,\boldsymbol\epsilon}(h)\le

307	      \prod_{i\in O_D}h_i\prod_{j\in C_D}h_j^{1-\alpha},
308	      &0<\alpha<1,\\[2mm]
309	      \displaystyle\left(\frac{c_\delta}{2}\right)^k
310	      \prod_{i\in O_D}h_i,&\alpha=1.
311	    \end{cases}

314	  \begin{equation}\label{E:d1-spatial-max}

322	  integral of the even decreasing function $|y|^{-\alpha}$ over an
323	  interval of fixed length is maximal when the interval is centered
324	  at zero. Therefore,
325	  \[
326	    \sup_z\int_\R G(h,y)c_\alpha|y+z|^{-\alpha}\ud y
327	    =\frac{c_\alpha h^{1-\alpha}}{1-\alpha}.

330	  $p_\epsilon(w)\ud w$ average of the unsmoothed integrals with shifts $z-w$.
331	  Its nonnegative mass-one average is therefore bounded by the same supremum. In
332	  the white case, $\gamma_\epsilon = c_\delta p_\epsilon$, so
333	  \[
334	    \sup_z\int_\R G(h,y)\gamma_\epsilon(y+z)\ud y

371	Define the total-order coefficients
372	\[
373	  A_k(t)=\sum_{m=0}^{2k}\E[X_m(t,x)X_{2k-m}(t,x)],\qquad A_0(t)=1.
374	\]
375	They do not depend on $x$, by spatial stationarity. By
376	Proposition~\ref{P:mixed}, $\E u^2(t,x) = \sum_{k\ge0}A_k(t)$.
377	
378	\begin{proposition}[One-dimensional upper bound]\label{P:d1-upper}
379	  Under~\eqref{E:d1-covariances}, for every $k \ge 1$ and $t > 0$,
380	  \begin{equation}\label{E:d1-coefficient}
381	    A_k(t)\le
382	    \frac{(2ZK_{\rm sp})^k t^{\beta k}}{k!\,k^{bk}}
383	    \le\frac{(2ZK_{\rm sp})^k t^{\beta k}}{(k!)^q}.
384	  \end{equation}
385	  Consequently,
386	  \begin{equation}\label{E:d1-upper}
387	    \E u^2(t,x)\le\exp(C_2t^\kappa),\qquad
388	    C_2=q(2ZK_{\rm sp})^{1/q},\quad \kappa=\frac{\beta}{q}.
389	  \end{equation}
390	\end{proposition}
391	
392	\begin{proof}
393	  We first work with the Gaussian spatial smoothing and temporal truncation
394	  in~\cite{chen:author2026:time-dependency}*{(2.9), (2.11), (2.23)--(2.24)}. Let
395	  $X_n^{\epsilon,\delta}$ be the smoothed Stratonovich term, using common
396	  parameters in every factor. Wick's formula expresses each mixed expectation of
397	  total order $2k$ as a sum over $D \in \Pi_k$. After the chain reversal in
398	  Proposition~\ref{P:mixed}, its spatial factor is the one in
399	  Lemma~\ref{L:d1-spatial}; its temporal factors are nonnegative and bounded by
400	  $|s_i-s_j|^{-\alpha_0}$. For times in $[0,t]^m_ < \times[0,t]^{2k-m}_ <$, the
401	  increments sum to the two terminal times and therefore to at most $2t$.
402	  Extract~\eqref{E:d1-spatial-max}, which is independent of the time vector, the
403	  split, the pairing, and the smoothing parameters. The remaining temporal sum
404	  is
405	  \[
406	    F_k(s_1,\ldots,s_{2k})
407	    =\sum_{D\in\Pi_k}\prod_{(i,j)\in D}|s_i-s_j|^{-\alpha_0}.
408	  \]
409	  Every permutation of the $2k$ labels bijects $\Pi_k$, so $F_k$ is fully
410	  symmetric. Moreover,
411	  \[
412	    \int_{[0,t]^2}|s-r|^{-\alpha_0}\ud s\ud r
413	    =Zt^{2-\alpha_0},\qquad
414	    \int_{[0,t]^{2k}}F_k(s)\ud s
415	    =P_k(Zt^{2-\alpha_0})^k<\infty.
416	  \]
417	  The second equality uses the disjoint endpoints of every pairing. Partitioning
418	  the time cube according to the order within each block now gives
419	  \begin{equation}\label{E:d1-time-symmetry}
420	    \int_{[0,t]^m_<\times[0,t]^{2k-m}_<}F_k(s)\ud s
421	    =\frac{P_k(Zt^{2-\alpha_0})^k}{m!(2k-m)!}.
422	  \end{equation}
423	  Ties have measure zero. Crucially, this symmetry is applied to the \emph{sum}
424	  of pairings after taking the common spatial bound, not to an individual
425	  temporally weighted diagram.
426	
427	  The number of pairings obeys $P_0 = 1$ and $P_k = (2k-1)P_{k-1}$, by choosing
428	  the partner of the smallest label. Hence, $P_k = (2k)!/(2^kk!)$. The binomial
429	  identity gives
430	  \[
431	    \sum_{m=0}^{2k}\frac1{m!(2k-m)!}=\frac{2^{2k}}{(2k)!}.
432	  \]
433	  Multiplying~\eqref{E:d1-time-symmetry} by the spatial bound and summing over
434	  $m$ yields
435	  \[
436	    \sum_{m=0}^{2k}\E[X_m^{\epsilon,\delta}X_{2k-m}^{\epsilon,\delta}]
437	    \le K_{\rm sp}^{\,k}\frac{t^{bk}}{k^{bk}}
438	    \frac{2^{2k}}{(2k)!}
439	    \frac{(2k)!}{2^kk!}(Zt^{2-\alpha_0})^k
440	    =\frac{(2ZK_{\rm sp})^kt^{\beta k}}{k!\,k^{bk}}.
441	  \]
442	  The same proof covers empty chains, with $X_0^{\epsilon,\delta} = 1$.
443	
444	  By Lemma~\ref{L:joint-fixed-order}, each smoothed factor converges in $L^2$.
445	  Products converge in $L^1$ by Cauchy--Schwarz; for fixed $k$ the sum over
446	  splits is finite. The bound is uniform in $\epsilon,\delta$, so it passes to
447	  $A_k(t)$. Since $k! \le k^k$ and $b > 0$, we have $k!\,k^{bk} \ge (k!)^{b+1} =
448	  (k!)^q$, proving both inequalities in~\eqref{E:d1-coefficient}.
449	
450	  Finally, for $z \ge 0$ and $q \ge 1$,
451	  \[
452	    \sum_{k\ge0}\frac{z^k}{(k!)^q}
453	    =\sum_{k\ge0}\left(\frac{z^{k/q}}{k!}\right)^q
454	    \le\left(\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{z^{k/q}}{k!}\right)^q
455	    =\exp(qz^{1/q}).
456	  \]
457	  Apply this inequality with $z = 2ZK_{\rm sp}t^\beta$, adding the separately
458	  defined term $A_0 = 1$. Proposition~\ref{P:mixed} then
459	  gives~\eqref{E:d1-upper}. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:d1-upper}.
460	\end{proof}

462	\subsection{Spectral bounds for $0 < \alpha \le 1$ in all three dimensions}
463	
464	We now retain Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} with $d \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $0 < \alpha
465	\le 1$. The covariance is nonnegative and nonnegative definite as in
466	Section~\ref{S:model}; when it is a distribution, both these properties and its
467	homogeneity are understood distributionally. Let $\mu$ be its positive Radon
468	spectral measure in the convention $\gamma(x) = \int e^{i\xi\cdot
469	x}\mu(\ud\xi)$, and put $V = \mu(\{\xi:|\xi|\le1\})$. No isotropy or spectral
470	density is assumed. Write $G_h$ for the positive wave-kernel measure of mass
471	$h$, and $G_{h,\eta} = p_\eta*G_h$ for $\eta > 0$; set $G_{h,0} = G_h$. The
472	measure notation includes the sphere kernel in dimension three. The mixed-moment
473	definition of $A_k(t)$ is now applied to the present $d$-dimensional solution.
474	
475	\begin{lemma}[Low-$\alpha$ convolution bound]\label{L:low-alpha-convolution}
476	  Under the preceding assumptions with $0 < \alpha < 1$, for every $R,h > 0$,
477	  \begin{equation}\label{E:low-alpha-radial}
478	    \mu(\{\xi:|\xi|\le R\})=VR^\alpha,\qquad
479	    \int_{\R^d}\min\{h,|\xi|^{-1}\}\mu(\ud\xi)
480	    =\frac{V}{1-\alpha}h^{1-\alpha}.
481	  \end{equation}
482	  For $\epsilon > 0$ and $\eta \ge 0$,
483	  \begin{equation}\label{E:low-alpha-convolution}
484	    0\le\int_{\R^d}G_{h,\eta}(\ud y)\gamma_\epsilon(y+z)
485	    \le\frac{V}{1-\alpha}h^{1-\alpha},
486	    \qquad z\in\R^d.
487	  \end{equation}
488	  The estimate is uniform in both smoothing parameters and in $z$.
489	\end{lemma}
490	
491	\begin{proof}
492	  The spectral measure of $\gamma(c\,\cdot)$ is the pushforward of $\mu$ under
493	  $\xi\mapsto c\xi$. Homogeneity and uniqueness of the Fourier transform on
494	  tempered distributions therefore give $\mu(A/c) = c^{-\alpha}\mu(A)$ for every
495	  Borel set $A$. Equivalently, $\mu(cA) = c^\alpha\mu(A)$. This proves the
496	  ball-mass formula. Since $\mu$ is Radon, $V < \infty$, and continuity from
497	  above gives $\mu(\{0\}) = \lim_{R\downarrow0}VR^\alpha = 0$. By the layer-cake
498	  identity and Tonelli's theorem,
499	  \[
500	    \int_{\R^d}\min\{h,|\xi|^{-1}\}\mu(\ud\xi)
501	    =\int_0^h\mu(\{\xi:|\xi|\le u^{-1}\})\ud u
502	    =V\int_0^h u^{-\alpha}\ud u.
503	  \]
504	  The endpoint of each indicator has no effect on its $u$ integral. Since
505	  $\alpha < 1$, the last expression is the finite quantity
506	  in~\eqref{E:low-alpha-radial}. This computation uses ball masses, not a radial
507	  density for $\mu$.
508	
509	  Gaussian weighting gives a finite measure, by the polynomial ball growth of
510	  $\mu$. Thus, Fourier Fubini is justified for $\gamma_\epsilon$ and the finite
511	  measure $G_{h,\eta}$. From the source's wave-kernel
512	  formulas~\cite{chen:author2026:time-dependency}*{(2.3)--(2.5), p.~7},
513	  \[
514	    \widehat{G}_h(\xi)=\frac{\sin(h|\xi|)}{|\xi|},\qquad
515	    G_h(\R^d)=h,
516	  \]
517	  with value $h$ in the Fourier formula at zero. The Fourier multipliers of
518	  $p_\epsilon$ and $p_\eta$ have absolute value at most one, with the latter
519	  multiplier equal to one when $\eta = 0$. Consequently,
520	  \[
521	    \left|\int G_{h,\eta}(\ud y)\gamma_\epsilon(y+z)\right|
522	    \le\int_{\R^d}\frac{|\sin(h|\xi|)|}{|\xi|}\mu(\ud\xi)
523	    \le\int_{\R^d}\min\{h,|\xi|^{-1}\}\mu(\ud\xi).
524	  \]
525	  Nonnegativity of $\gamma$ as a distribution implies $\gamma_\epsilon \ge 0$,
526	  since Gaussian translates are nonnegative test functions; $G_{h,\eta}$ is also
527	  nonnegative. This proves the lower bound in~\eqref{E:low-alpha-convolution}.
528	  Combining the preceding displays proves its upper bound. No positivity of the
529	  oscillatory Fourier integrand is asserted. This proves
530	  Lemma~\ref{L:low-alpha-convolution}.
531	\end{proof}
532	
533	\begin{lemma}[Degree-one convolution bound]\label{L:alpha-one-convolution}
534	  Under the preceding covariance assumptions with $\alpha = 1$, for every $h >
535	  0$, $\epsilon > 0$, $\eta \ge 0$, and $z \in \R^d$,
536	  \begin{equation}\label{E:alpha-one-convolution}
537	    0\le\int_{\R^d}G_{h,\eta}(\ud y)\gamma_\epsilon(y+z)
538	    \le\frac{\pi V}{2}.
539	  \end{equation}
540	  No isotropy or angular density is required.
541	\end{lemma}
542	
543	\begin{proof}
544	  Fourier uniqueness, applied to the distributional homogeneity as above, gives
545	  $\mu(cA) = c\mu(A)$ and $\mu(\{0\}) = 0$. Define a finite measure on the unit
546	  sphere by
547	  \[
548	    \sigma(E)=\mu\{\xi:0<|\xi|\le1,\ \xi/|\xi|\in E\}.
549	  \]
550	  Its total mass is $V$. Homogeneity implies that the corresponding sector of
551	  radius $R$ has mass $R\sigma(E)$. Subtracting two such sectors shows that a
552	  polar rectangle $(r_1,r_2]\times E$ has mass $(r_2-r_1)\sigma(E)$. Uniqueness
553	  of measures on these generating rectangles therefore gives the polar
554	  decomposition $\mu(\ud\xi) = \ud r\,\sigma(\ud\theta)$, $r > 0$, $\theta \in
555	  \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. The real stationary covariance is even; Fourier uniqueness
556	  makes $\mu$, and hence $\sigma$, even.
557	
558	  Use the Brownian Gaussian convention, so the combined covariance and Green
559	  smoothing multiplier is $e^{-ar^2}$ with $a = (\epsilon+\eta)/2 > 0$. Gaussian
560	  weighting makes the spectral measure finite. Fourier Fubini and evenness give
561	  \begin{equation}\label{E:alpha-one-polar}
562	    \begin{split}
563	      \int G_{h,\eta}(\ud y)\gamma_\epsilon(y+z)
564	      &=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} I_a(h,\theta\cdot z)\sigma(\ud\theta),\\
565	      I_a(h,v)&=\int_0^\infty e^{-ar^2}
566	      \frac{\sin(hr)}r\cos(rv)\ud r.
567	    \end{split}
568	  \end{equation}
569	  The radial integral is absolutely convergent: its integrand is bounded near
570	  zero and Gaussian-decaying at infinity. Passing from the complex exponential
571	  to cosine introduces no factor two, since both antipodal directions are
572	  already included in $\sigma$.
573	
574	  Let $g_h(v) = \tfrac12\mathbf1_{\{|v|<h\}}$ and let $p_{2a}^{(1)}(v) = (4\pi
575	  a)^{-1/2}e^{-v^2/(4a)}$ be the one-dimensional Gaussian density. Their Fourier
576	  transforms are $\sin(hr)/r$ and $e^{-ar^2}$. The one-dimensional inversion
577	  factor is $1/(2\pi)$ in the source convention, so
578	  \[
579	    (g_h*p_{2a}^{(1)})(v)
580	    =\frac1{2\pi}\int_\R e^{irv}e^{-ar^2}
581	    \frac{\sin(hr)}r\ud r
582	    =\frac1\pi I_a(h,v).
583	  \]
584	  The sign in the inversion exponential is immaterial because the integrand
585	  pairs evenly under $r\mapsto-r$. Since $p_{2a}^{(1)}$ has mass one and $0 \le
586	  g_h \le 1/2$, we obtain $0 \le I_a(h,v) \le \pi/2$. Integrating against
587	  $\sigma$, whose mass is $V$, proves~\eqref{E:alpha-one-convolution}. This
588	  retains the oscillation until the one-dimensional integral is evaluated; the
589	  divergent absolute Fourier envelope at $\alpha = 1$ is not used. This proves
590	  Lemma~\ref{L:alpha-one-convolution}.
591	\end{proof}

594	  Suppose that Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} and the standing covariance positivity
595	  assumptions hold, $d \in \{1,2,3\}$, $0 < \alpha \le 1$, and $V > 0$. Define
596	  \begin{equation}\label{E:low-alpha-constants}
597	    \begin{split}
598	      K_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen}
599	      &=\begin{cases}
600	        \displaystyle\frac{V2^{2-\alpha}(1-\alpha)^{-\alpha}}
601	        {(2-\alpha)^{2-\alpha}},&0<\alpha<1,\\[2mm]
602	        \pi V,&\alpha=1,
603	      \end{cases}\\
604	      C_2^{\rm gen}&=q(2ZK_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen})^{1/q}.
605	    \end{split}

608	  $k \ge 1$ and $t > 0$,
609	  \begin{equation}\label{E:low-alpha-coefficient}
610	    A_k(t)\le\frac{(2ZK_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen})^k t^{\beta k}}
611	    {k!\,k^{bk}}
612	    \le\frac{(2ZK_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen})^k t^{\beta k}}{(k!)^q},

614	    \E u^2(t,x)\le\exp(C_2^{\rm gen}t^\kappa).

617	
618	\begin{proof}
619	  First smooth the noise as in~\cite{chen:author2026:time-dependency}*{(2.9), (2.11), (2.23)--(2.24)}.
620	  In dimension three also use $G_{h,\eta}$ with $\eta > 0$, as in the
621	  source's pp.~13--14. The increment change of variables is now a
622	  triangular map on vectors in $\R^d$, still of determinant one.
623	  The descending-label proof of Lemma~\ref{L:d1-spatial} depends only
624	  on which increments enter each position, not on their dimension.
625	  Its invariant therefore remains valid: at a closing label there
626	  is exactly one covariance depending on that vector increment, and
627	  at an opening label its pair has already been removed.
628	  If $0 < \alpha < 1$, Lemma~\ref{L:low-alpha-convolution} gives the
629	  closing bound $Mh_l^{1-\alpha}$ with $M = V/(1-\alpha)$.
630	  At $\alpha = 1$, Lemma~\ref{L:alpha-one-convolution} gives the
631	  constant closing bound $M = \pi V/2$. Every opening gives mass
632	  $h_l$, uniformly in $\eta$ and all noise-smoothing parameters.
633	  For $\alpha < 1$, the same weighted arithmetic--geometric mean
634	  calculation gives
635	  \[
636	    M^k\prod_{i\in O_D}h_i\prod_{j\in C_D}h_j^{1-\alpha}
637	    \le (K_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen})^k\frac{t^{bk}}{k^{bk}}.
638	  \]
639	  At $\alpha = 1$, ordinary arithmetic--geometric mean on the $k$ opening
640	  increments gives $M^k\prod_{i\in O_D}h_i \le (2M)^kt^k/k^k$, which is the same
641	  bound with $b = 1$ and $K_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen} = \pi V$. Both cases use
642	  $\sum_lh_l \le 2t$. For $d = 1,2$ one may use the Green densities directly;
643	  their opening mass and closing convolution obey these same bounds.
644	
645	  Replace the nonnegative truncated temporal factors by $|s_i-s_j|^{-\alpha_0}$
646	  before taking their pairing sum. The temporal symmetry, cube integral and
647	  split count in~\eqref{E:d1-time-symmetry} do not involve the spatial
648	  dimension. Thus, exactly the multiplication of counts in the proof of
649	  Proposition~\ref{P:d1-upper} gives the first bound
650	  in~\eqref{E:low-alpha-coefficient} for the regularized moments.
651	
652	  We spell out the limit in dimension three. Fix every noise-smoothing parameter

654	  formula is a finite sum of bounded continuous products of the smoothed

696	\begin{corollary}[First-moment calibration]\label{C:d1-first-calibration}
697	  Let $K_*$ be $K_{\rm sp}$ under~\eqref{E:d1-covariances}, or $K_{\rm sp}^{\rm
698	  gen}$ under the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{P:low-alpha-upper}. Put
699	  $C_{2,*} = q(2ZK_*)^{1/q}$. Then
700	  \begin{equation}\label{E:d1-first-calibration}
701	    \E u(t,x)\le\exp(C_{1,*}t^\kappa),\qquad
702	    C_{1,*}=q\left(\frac{ZK_*}{2^{3-\alpha}}\right)^{1/q}
703	    =\frac{C_{2,*}}{2^{(4-\alpha)/(3-\alpha)}}.
704	  \end{equation}
705	  In either nonzero case $2C_{1,*} < C_{2,*}$. Conditionally on a first-moment
706	  lower rate at least $L_*$, $2L_* \le 2C_{1,*} < C_{2,*}$, consistently with
707	  Proposition~\ref{P:Jensen}.
708	\end{corollary}
709	
710	\begin{proof}
711	  For one chain of length $2k$, the increments sum to at most $t$. The spatial
712	  estimate in Lemma~\ref{L:d1-spatial}, or in the proof of
713	  Proposition~\ref{P:low-alpha-upper}, therefore applies with $t/2$ in place of
714	  $t$. The temporal pairing sum on one ordered simplex is
715	  $P_k(Zt^{2-\alpha_0})^k/(2k)!$. Using the same regularization and limit order
716	  as in the respective upper-bound proof gives
717	  \[
718	    \E X_{2k}(t,x)
719	    \le\frac{(ZK_*/2^{b+1})^k t^{\beta k}}{k!\,k^{bk}}
720	    \le\frac{(ZK_*/2^{3-\alpha})^k t^{\beta k}}{(k!)^q}.
721	  \]
722	  Every odd term has zero expectation. The $L^2$ expansion permits taking
723	  expectations of partial sums, and the resulting nonnegative even series is
724	  summed by the scalar inequality in the proof of Proposition~\ref{P:d1-upper}.
725	  This gives~\eqref{E:d1-first-calibration}. If the first-moment lower rate is
726	  at least $L_*$, \eqref{E:d1-first-calibration} implies $L_* \le C_{1,*}$. In
727	  the stated nonzero cases $K_* > 0$, hence $C_{1,*} > 0$; and
728	  $(4-\alpha)/(3-\alpha) > 1$ gives $2C_{1,*} < C_{2,*}$. This proves
729	  Corollary~\ref{C:d1-first-calibration}.
730	\end{proof}

804	\begin{align}

818	\begin{proposition}[Uniform scalar row]\label{P:frequency-row}

820	  $\xi$, such that

830	  pushforward under $\lambda \mapsto \eta = \xi-\lambda$. Then $\nu_\xi(B(0,R))

838	  \[

844	  \begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-inverse-bessel}
